title: Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from Sky-Fever game after confrontation
content:
CHICAGO — Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was escorted out of Wintrust Arena on Sunday night after Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud confronted him at his courtside baseline seat during the team’s game against the Indiana Fever.

Late in the third quarter, Cloud scored on a driving layup, prompting a timeout from the Fever. The veteran guard approached Freedom, who has gained notoriety for his vocal opposition to transgender athletes competing in women’s sports.

A member of Indiana team security restrained Cloud — the incident occurred across from the Fever team bench — while multiple security officials walked Freedom out of the arena bowl and into the lobby.

As Freedom walked out, he tugged at a shirt that read “WOMAN noun adult human female” and egged on jeers from the crowd.

“I’m supporting women, and that is the reason they’re kicking me out,” Freedom told a group of arena officials and law enforcement officers in the Wintrust Arena lobby. “It’s unacceptable.”

In early August, Freedom announced his intention to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft to challenge the support of transgender women playing in the league.

Freedom, 34, played 748 games across 11 NBA seasons before being waived by the Houston Rockets in February of 2022, effectively ending his career in the league. He claimed at the time that he was waived for his views about the Chinese government, an accusation NBA commissioner Adam Silver denied.

Tricia Smith, a fan who said she sat next to Freedom for the entire game to that point, said Cloud instigated the confrontation.

“Natasha Cloud scored. She came over and threw her hands up and was talking s— to his face,” said Smith, a Boise, Idaho, native, who said she didn’t know Freedom before the game. “So he stood up and said like, ‘What? What do you want?’ He didn’t do a thing. I’ve sat next to him the whole game. He’s a great guy. He’s taken probably 50 pictures tonight.”

He was heckled outside of the arena as well before the game. Cloud was not at the Sky’s postgame news conference, but Sky coach Tyler Marsh supported his player in the immediate aftermath.

“Tash didn’t want to feel like she was a distraction, I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects the people that need to be protected. And so Tash is always going to stand on that, and then we stand for Tash.”

For their part, the Fever contingent that appeared for a postgame news conference — head coach Stephanie White and players Caitlin Clark and Lexie Hull — said they didn’t see the incident transpire.

“We were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Clark said after putting up 37 points and 10 assists — her fourth 30-point, 10-assist performance of the season.

Still, for Indiana, it was another non-basketball controversy that distracted from its on-floor production — and a much-needed win Sunday to stop a two-game losing skid. Of this latest episode, White said it was “important” that the media and general public “don’t give it any gas.”

“It’s a social media thing,” White said.

No transgender athletes compete in the WNBA, but the topic has hovered over the league since an ESPN article in July in which Fever guard Sophie Cunningham came out against transgender participation in women’s sports. Small rallies have since popped up outside arenas at Fever road games in support of Cunningham, and have been met with counter demonstrations in support of trans athletes.

Fans inside arenas at a Dream game wearing shirts expressing support and exclusion of trans athletes were asked to cover them, according to the league, and the Seattle Storm owner was suspended and fined by the WNBA after an exchange with two teenage girls wearing shirts depicting XX and XY chromosomes.

Sabreena Merchant contributed to this story.
